theme: Babylon’s gods fail; “I have called you by name”
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 46:1-49:26. Babylon’s gods are carried off on wagons, Babylon herself falls, and the Servant speaks in the first person. Notice the contrast between a god who must be carried and a God who carries.
settingTheScene: The prophet speaks to exiles who see the glittering idols of Babylon every day. Chapters 46 and 47 contrast the gods who are carried with the God who carries, and announce the fall of proud Babylon. In chapters 48 and 49, God exhorts a stubborn people, and the second Servant Song appears. Here the Servant speaks for himself, and we learn that his work is larger than Israel.
observation: “Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are loaded as burdens on weary beasts” (46:1).
“Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (46:4).
“I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning” (46:9-10).
“You said, I shall be mistress forever” (47:7).
“I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go” (48:17).
“The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name” (49:1).
“It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob… I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (49:6).
“Can a woman forget her nursing child… Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (49:15-16).
interpretation:
Chapter 46 gives a stark image. The great gods of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, are loaded onto animals and carted off into captivity. Idols are heavy burdens that have to be carried, and they cannot save. Over against them is the God who carries: “I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.” The difference between the true God and the false is the difference between a weight and a carrier. One needs to be carried by us. The other carries us, from birth to gray hairs.

Chapter 47 is a taunt song against Babylon, depicted as a pampered queen who sits on a throne and is told to sit in the dust. She thought, “I am, and there is no one besides me,” a boast that belongs only to God. Her sorcerers and astrologers cannot save her. The pride that exalts itself to the place of God is brought low.

In chapter 48, God addresses the stubborn exiles who invoke his name but not in truth. He declares the future before it happens so that they cannot say their idols did it. And he laments: “Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river.” Yet he will bring them out: “Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea.”

Chapter 49 introduces the Servant speaking, “Listen to me, O coastlands.” He was called before birth, his mouth made like a sharp sword, hidden in the shadow of God’s hand. Strikingly, he says, “I have labored in vain.” Yet his work is given to God. The commission is expanded: it is too light a thing to restore Israel alone. He will be “a light for the nations.” The Servant’s mission is global.

The chapter ends with the loveliest assurance. Zion says, “The LORD has forsaken me.” God answers that a mother may forget her nursing child, but he will not forget. “I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.” The hands that were scarred are the hands that remember.
connection: Simeon quoted Isaiah 49:6 when he held the infant Jesus and called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). Paul and Barnabas applied it to their mission in Acts 13:47. In John 8:12, Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.” The scars on the hands of Jesus (John 20:27) are the true fulfillment of “engraved on the palms of my hands.” Revelation 18 shows the fall of Babylon the great.
application:
Name something you are carrying that you were never meant to carry, and give it to the God who carries.

Read Isaiah 49:15-16 slowly, and let it reassure you if you feel forgotten.

Pray for the spread of the gospel to the ends of the earth, as the Servant’s mission calls.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he will carry you to your old age.
Thank him that you are engraved on the palms of his hands.
Tell him what idol you are tempted to carry yourself.
